title: Lebkuchen
subtitle: German spiced Christmas biscuits with a sugar glaze
excerpt: Lebkuchen are soft, chewy German spiced biscuits made with honey and ground almonds. You get biscuits that stay moist and improve over the days after baking. Watch the baking time: they look underdone when they come out but firm to the right texture as they cool.
sourceNotes: Lebkuchen originate in the medieval German monastic baking tradition, with the city of Nuremberg (Nürnberger Lebkuchen) being the most historically documented centre of production (PGI-protected since 1996). The recipe here follows the standard home-baking form: honey, mixed spice, cinnamon, ground almonds, and a simple icing-sugar glaze.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the unglazed biscuits for up to 3 months. Glaze after defrosting at room temperature.
recipe.batchNotes: The dough can be made in double quantity and refrigerated for up to 3 days before rolling.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Lebkuchen improve significantly over 2 to 3 days as the spices develop and the texture softens further. Make at least a day ahead of when you want to eat them.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 170 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 155 degrees Celsius. Middle shelf.

glossaryTerms.definition: A pre-blended British spice mixture typically containing coriander, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, and allspice. In Lebkuchen it works alongside cinnamon to provide the characteristic warm, complex flavour. The exact blend varies by brand; a stronger mixture will give more pronounced spice flavour.

A thin coating of icing sugar dissolved in water, applied to the still-warm biscuit so it dries to a thin, glossy white layer. The glaze seals the biscuit surface, slows moisture loss, and gives Lebkuchen their characteristic appearance. Apply it thinly with a pastry brush while the biscuits are warm so the glaze spreads evenly.

content.text: Warm the honey, butter, and soft brown sugar in a medium saucepan over low heat, stirring until the butter has melted and the sugar dissolved. Remove from the heat and leave to cool until just warm, about 10 minutes.
Beat the egg into the cooled mixture. Stir in the orange zest. Sift in the flour, bicarbonate of soda,
, and cinnamon, then add the ground almonds. Mix to a soft, slightly sticky dough.
Flatten the dough into a disc, wrap, and refrigerate for at least 1 hour until firm enough to roll. The dough can be left in the fridge overnight.

Preheat the oven to 170 degrees Celsius. Line two baking trays with baking paper. If using wafer circles, place them on the trays and pipe or spoon a small amount of dough onto each one instead of cutting.
Roll the dough out on a lightly floured surface to about 5 to 6 mm thickness. Cut into rounds or decorative shapes with biscuit cutters. Place on the lined trays, leaving 2 cm between them.

Bake for 13 to 15 minutes. The biscuits should be firm at the edges and just set in the centre; they will look slightly underdone. They firm up further as they cool. Remove from the oven and leave on the trays for 5 minutes.
Mix the icing sugar with the warm water to make a thin
. It should be thin enough to brush but not watery. While the biscuits are still warm, brush the glaze generously over the top of each one. Leave on a cooling rack until the glaze is completely dry.

attrs.problem: The dough is too soft and sticky to roll
attrs.avoid: Avoid rolling the dough before it has chilled for the full hour; honey-based doughs are very soft at room temperature.
attrs.fix: Return the dough to the fridge for a further 30 minutes. Dust the work surface and rolling pin well with flour and work quickly. If the dough warms and sticks again mid-rolling, chill it for another 15 minutes before continuing.

attrs.problem: The biscuits are hard rather than soft and chewy
attrs.avoid: Avoid overbaking; these biscuits should come out of the oven looking slightly underdone.
attrs.fix: Remove the biscuits from the oven as soon as the edges are set and the tops look barely done. They will firm further as they cool. Store in an airtight tin; the texture softens again after 24 hours as the honey re-distributes moisture.

attrs.problem: The glaze is streaky or blotchy
attrs.avoid: Avoid applying the glaze to biscuits that have fully cooled; the glaze sets before it can spread evenly.
attrs.fix: Apply the glaze while the biscuits are still warm. Thin the glaze slightly with a few drops of warm water if it is thickening as you work. Brush in one smooth pass rather than going back over the same area multiple times.
